narrative.morphology: Solitary planktonic trichomes, straight or slightly curved, several hundred µm long, 3-4 µm wide, with bluntly rounded or slightly tapered end cells; scarcely constricted at the cross walls (Plates 1, 2). Vegetative cells are cylindrical, 1-3 times longer than wide, at the ends of the trichome, up to 6-7 times longer than wide, gradually becoming longer and often reaching 25-30 µm in length; with gas vesicles.
narrative.ecology: Umezakia ovalisporum, a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium invaded Lake Kinneret in 1994 (Pollingher et al. 1998), shortly after the Hula Valley was hydrologically disconnected from Lake Kinneret when Lake Agmon was created (Hambright and Zohary 1998). This disconnection reduced substantially the nitrate load entering Lake Kinneret and created in-lake conditions suitable for the proliferation of nitrogen fixers. Umezakia ovalisporum was the first of several species of nostocalean cyanobacteria never recorded previously that appeared in Lake Kinneret since 1994 and got established in the lake. In September-October 1994 U. ovalisporum formed a massive bloom in Kinneret (Fig. 1). Since 1994 it is a common component of the Kinneret summer phytoplankton. It occurs in the plankton only when the lake is stratified, peaking in September-October (Fig. 2). Towards the onset of winter, it forms akinetes (Plate 1) that sink to the sediment and wait for germination till the following summer. This species is usually evenly distributed throughout the epilimnion. In Kinneret it doesn’t form surface films and doesn’t cluster.
narrative.environmental_conditions:
Umezakia ovalisporum disappears when the pH exceeds 9 (Fig. 3) although its intense blooms push the pH towards this level. It is adapted to higher salinities, higher water temperatures, lower TP levels. In lab experiments, A. ovalisporum hardly grew under Na+ lower than 2.5 mM (Bar Yosef thesis, P.9, based on Kaplan et al. 1984. FEBS letters 176:166-168).
